planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this chance Bernese seedling needs a compatible pollinizer and rewards patient cellar storage.

directions: Berner Rosenapfel arose as a chance seedling discovered around 1890 near Oppligen in the canton of Bern, Switzerland, a cross between Roter Winter-Calvill and the older local cider apple Sauergrauech. The fruit is juicy and notably sweet with a spicy, aromatic edge that sets it apart from its tart parent. Harvest falls in mid-October, and the apples keep in a cool cellar in good condition until February. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer nearby, and prune to an open framework for even ripening.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; grow chiefly as a juice and cider apple rather than a fresh-eating type.

directions: Sauergrauech has been grown in the canton of Bern, Switzerland since at least the 18th century and is one of the oldest documented cider apples in the region. The relatively small, gray-russeted fruit is fruity and brightly aromatic with a refreshing acidity that makes it especially prized for pressing into juice, though it can also go into desserts or be eaten fresh when fully ripe. It later became a parent of the sweeter Berner Rosenapfel. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer, and expect a long-lived, productive tree typical of old Swiss orchard stock.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this is a cider and perry pear, not a dessert type, and needs a compatible pollinizer.

directions: Schweizer Wasserbirne, also known locally as Kugelbirne, Glockenbirne, or Thurgauerbirne, has been widely planted across Switzerland and southern Germany since the 19th century as a dedicated cider and perry pear. The large, almost spherical fruit has smooth yellow-green skin that dulls to red on the sun-exposed side, and it ripens in mid-October on a big, vigorous tree. It presses into an abundant volume of clear, pale juice, though the resulting cider is light-bodied and does not keep as well as cider from firmer varieties. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer, allowing ample room for the tree's eventual large size.
sources: Netzwerk Streuobst Filderstadt orchard variety database

planting.note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4 inches deep in cool, fertile mountain-garden soil; hill as the stems grow and expect low yields of small, flavorful tubers.

directions: Parli is a small, high-altitude heirloom potato documented since around 1850 between the Prättigau and Safiental valleys in the Swiss canton of Graubünden, named for an old Walser family line. Its small tubers are prized by cooks for a rich, chestnut-like flavor, though the plant is a low, somewhat difficult yielder that has kept it rare even among heritage growers. Modern seed stock is distributed almost entirely through Swiss heritage conservation programs working to keep it in a handful of mountain gardens and select restaurants. Grow in cool, well-drained soil with full sun, and accept a lighter harvest in exchange for exceptional flavor.
sources: ECPGR In Situ Landraces Best Practice Database

planting.note: Drill or broadcast as a winter grain in early fall, sowing earlier at high mountain elevations; this landrace tillers heavily and resists lodging on lean alpine ground.

directions: Binnegga is a traditional winter rye landrace from the village of Grengiols in the Valais region of Switzerland, historically grown on lean, dry terraced fields at elevations up to roughly 6,500 feet in the Central Alps. It produces long, well-formed yellow grain on plants that tiller profusely from a single kernel and stand reliably well against wind and weather in thin mountain soil. Because it thrives on minimal fertility, it needs none of the rich feeding modern grains expect, and it has long supplied flour for the dense, dark rye breads of the Valais. Sow as a fall-planted winter grain and let it overwinter as a low rosette before it resumes growth and heads out the following summer.
sources: Erschmatt Roggenwelt heritage grain conservation project

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm and frost danger has passed; set sturdy poles for this vigorous climber and let some pods dry fully on the vine for shelling.

directions: Chriesistei, Swiss German for cherry pit, is an old dual-purpose pole bean once widely grown across the canton of Aargau, named for its small, round, dark red to purplish-blue seeds that resemble cherry stones. Several local strains tied to individual villages persisted alongside the main type as farm families kept their own seed lines. The vigorous vines are picked young as green snap beans or left on the pole to dry fully for shelling and winter storage. Grow in warm, fertile soil in full sun on sturdy poles, watering consistently through flowering and pod set.
sources: Bohnen-Atlas Swiss and German bean variety database

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; this classic Swiss garden bean climbs vigorously and benefits from tall, sturdy support.

directions: Weinländerin, also sold under its French name La Vigneronne, is a classic old Swiss pole bean long cultivated and passed down by countrywomen gardeners. Its pods are streaked and speckled with purple as though stained by drops of wine, giving the variety both its German and French names. The vigorous vines are productive over a long season and can be picked young for snap beans or allowed to mature for dry shelling beans. Give it full sun, consistent moisture, and sturdy poles, since this old variety climbs well beyond typical modern pole bean height.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into loose, deep soil; roots improve in flavor and texture the longer they are left to mature, holding in the ground well into autumn.

directions: Küttiger Rüebli is an old, robust carrot named for the Aargau village of Küttigen, where it was already a market staple sold at the Aarau weekly market in the 19th century. The roots are large, conical, and white rather than orange, with an earthy, aromatic flavor that is notably not very sweet compared to modern carrots. Farmers traditionally sowed it directly alongside oats so that both crops could be tended and harvested together, and it was long kept alive by a local countrywomen's association before being taken up by Swiss heritage seed conservation. Sow directly into loose, deep soil in early spring and thin to allow the roots room to size up.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this old Baltic variety is best managed on a regular pruning schedule to avoid the scab problems that plague neglected trees.

directions: Lietuvos Pepinas is an old apple of uncertain origin dating to at least the 18th century, claimed as a heritage variety by both Lithuania and Belarus and also grown in Poland, where it is called Glogierówka, and in Latvia, where orchardists often simply call it the pippin. The yellow-skinned fruit has white flesh with a distinctive vinous flavor, and well-tended trees were once described by orchardists as a genuine gold mine for yield and quality, though neglected trees tend to produce small, scab-marked fruit. It remains especially valued today for processing, pressing into a dark ruby wine with a pleasant apple-and-almond aroma and making excellent juice. Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil and keep up a regular pruning and disease-management routine to get the best fruit.
sources: Latvia State Institute of Fruit-Growing and Horticulture (Dobele) apple variety profiles
MDPI Molecules: Phenolic Compositions of Fruits of Lithuanian Heirloom Apple Cultivars (2020)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this moderately cold-hardy Samogitian variety forms a dense, rounded crown and bears well once established.

directions: Žemaičių Grietininis is a traditional autumn apple that spread through the Žemaitija, or Samogitia, region of western Lithuania, formally registered on Lithuania's national plant variety list in both 1899 and 1958. The medium-sized, roundly conical fruit has white to whitish-green skin streaked with red on the sun-facing side, enclosing white to yellowish-white flesh that is very juicy with a sweet-tart, wine-like flavor. It is harvested from late August into early September and keeps in ordinary storage until December, with moderate resistance to scab and good tolerance of handling and transport. Plant on a vigorous rootstock in full sun and expect heavier cropping to begin three to four years after planting.
sources: Lithuanian Research Centre for Agriculture and Forestry (LAMMC) pomology records
